title: India Cancels Norwegian Journalist's Visa Hours Before Hyderabad Summit Trip
excerpt: Helle Lyng Svendsen of Dagsavisen says her visa was cancelled minutes before departure for a press-freedom panel. The Editors Guild and CPJ have sought an explanation; the government had not publicly given one as of November 13.
body:
• Norwegian journalist Helle Lyng Svendsen says India cancelled her visa on November 11, about 10 minutes before she was due to leave for the airport to travel to the Bharat Summit in Hyderabad.
  • Svendsen had a valid single-entry visa and political clearance to speak on a panel on the future of media and press freedom, according to her account and the Editors Guild of India.
  • The Editors Guild and the Committee to Protect Journalists have asked India to explain and reverse the cancellation; as of November 13, neither the Home Ministry nor the External Affairs Ministry had publicly explained it.
  • Svendsen and the Guild link the move in their statements to her questioning of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Oslo in May — a motive the government has not confirmed.

India cancelled the visa of Norwegian journalist Helle Lyng Svendsen shortly before she was due to travel to Hyderabad to speak at the Bharat Summit, according to Svendsen and the Editors Guild of India. Svendsen, a commentator with the Oslo-based newspaper Dagsavisen, said the Indian Embassy in Oslo called her on November 11, about 10 minutes before she was to leave for the airport, and told her she would not be permitted to enter India. An email subsequently confirmed the cancellation.

In a video message posted on November 11 and addressed to Home Minister Amit Shah, Svendsen said she had been invited as a panellist and speaker on the future of media and press freedom. She said: "I got a visa to India and was supposed to leave this morning to attend the Bharat Summit in Hyderabad." She added that "orders from above" in the Ministry of Home Affairs had cancelled her visa. Those are her words for what embassy officials told her; the Home Ministry has not publicly confirmed that description or given its own reasons.

"No journalist should be targeted for asking critical questions."

— Committee to Protect Journalists, statement on the cancellation

What had been cleared before the cancellation

Svendsen said the summit organisers had obtained political clearance for her participation. She said she submitted documents on November 5 and was told on November 10 that her passport, with the Indian visa, was ready for collection. The Editors Guild said she held a valid single-entry visa for the duration of the summit and that the Ministry of External Affairs had cleared the names of foreign nationals attending the summit on November 3, with the clearance letter noting that approval from the Home Ministry and other authorities was also required. The Guild said the embassy asked her to visit in person to have the visa physically cancelled.

The Bharat Summit, organised by the Congress-led Telangana government, is being held on November 13 and 14 in Hyderabad. The AIDEM, citing The Wire, reported 113 foreign delegates had been denied permission to enter India for the summit — a figure The Videshi has not independently verified.

The Oslo exchange in May

Six months earlier, on May 18, 2026, Svendsen questioned Modi during his visit to Norway. At a joint media appearance with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre in Oslo, she called out as Modi was leaving the podium: "Prime Minister Modi, why don't you take some questions from the freest press in the world?" Modi walked away without responding, and video of the exchange circulated widely on social media.

Svendsen has said she believes the decision may be linked to that questioning, to her later criticism of the government, and to her questioning of industrialists Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani. Those are her stated suspicions, not a confirmed official reason.

Reactions and the government response so far

The Editors Guild, in a November 12 statement signed by president Sanjay Kapoor and general secretary Raghavan Srinivasan, said it could not understand the reason, described Svendsen as a legitimate and respected journalist, and called the move bureaucratic overreach. It demanded the government disclose the reasons and reverse the decision.

The Committee to Protect Journalists described the cancellation as likely retaliation, urged authorities to reinstate her visa and said India has a special responsibility to uphold press freedom. Congress, hosting the summit, also criticised the exclusion.

On the government side, the reported position is silence so far. The Wire reported that it sought a response from the Ministry of External Affairs and the Ministry of Home Affairs on the reasons for the cancellation and had received none at the time of publication, and The AIDEM reported on the morning of November 13 that neither ministry had publicly explained the decision. Until an official reason is given, the confirmed facts are the cancellation itself and its timing; the reason for it remains alleged, not established.
